title: The velocity of war and why faster isn't always smarter
subtitle: It's not the fall that kills you, it's the hitting the ground
author: Andy Owen
introduction: The winners of wars are the quickest to innovate, the fastest to reach technological milestones. Progress depends on speed. And now this dynamic is driving the race in AI. Here, former British Intelligence officer Andy Owen argues that we must slow down technological progress. Every new technology brings its own dangers, and currently we do not have the ability to account for or predict the risks. Furthermore, Owen argues, technology will never replace human thought, or a million and one of the other things we value; treating it as though it can will only lead to ruin. The race is not worth the risk.
body:
Writing almost 50 years ago, in Speed and Politics, Paul Virilio argued that the strategy and technology of war are the primary accelerators of human progress through the pursuit of velocity. Virilio’s dromology (science of speed) presciently described the impact of new technologies on war and an accelerating society. Virilio’s work also provides insight into the reaction to rapidity: the warfare of deceleration.

Virilio asserted that history is driven not by economics or class struggle. Power belongs to whoever controls velocity and the capacity to move fastest from identifying a target to having a destructive effect on it. Military logistics designs and produces the speed systems that can achieve this. They then orient society towards the production of systems that come to dictate civilian life.

In Crepuscular Dawn, Virilio sketches out three revolutions of speed. Firstly, the transport revolution, focusing on physical movement across terrestrial space and geopolitical boundaries from “metabolic bodies” of soldiers to the development of engines, trains, and automobiles, to ballistics capable of delivering nuclear warheads across continents, thus rendering the whole globe the battlefield. Secondly, the transmission revolution of telecommunications and computers, which collapses physical distance, replacing localized space with simultaneous electronic cyberspace. Lastly, he foresaw a transplantation revolution, characterized by the miniaturization of technology, increasing the speed of informational ingestion by feeding it directly into humans by “micromachines.”

SUGGESTED VIEWING The rules of war With Malcolm Rifkind, Mary Ann Sieghart, Bronwen Maddox, Yanis Varoufakis, Jeremy Corbyn

These revolutions lead to a “Dromocratic” State, where political control shifts from managing people in a fixed space to controlling the speed of movement and communication. The nation-state decays as technological speed renders borders obsolete. Acceleration replaces territorial sovereignty and democratic governance with global surveillance technology, the tyranny of automated systems, and logistics-based power.

The multi-matrixed world we are now in, as the post-1945 order fragments and barriers are going up, sees Virilo’s decaying but not yet obsolete nation-states forming complex, often contradictory, matrices of alliances across trade, security, energy, and cultural communality. Rather than rigid alliance blocs, states are situated in complex, web-like matrices of overlapping agreements, while attempting to resist the gravitational pull of regional powers engaged in global competition. States attempt to hedge rather than choose sides, motivated by survival and mutual benefit rather than ideology. These matrices are actively reordering security alliances, trade flows, and financial architectures. Struggling to maintain sovereignty, countries routinely develop partnerships with actors who do not share their values. Partners in one arena are direct adversaries in another. Alliances are transactional, overlapping, subject to rapid realignment, and reaching complexities that the diplomats and politicians charged with managing them are unable to comprehend. Woven into these alliances are powerful multinational companies, for years seen as rootless concentrations of stateless capital, but now increasingly being pulled back into geopolitics—not the old geopolitics of sovereign states asserting dominion—rather a relationship of mutual possession.

This symbiosis is only now being slowly understood by politicians and citizens who, having spent increasingly more time in the layer, came to see it as separate from the underlying physical reality it is situated in.

On top of the security alliances of physical armed forces, trade flows of physical goods, energy production from physical fuels and processes, and financial architectures of the multi-matrixed world that stretches from the deep ocean to the edges of space, new technologies have created a layer of virtualization. A product of Virilio’s transmission revolution, it near-comprehensively covers the topography, a digital stratus cloud, allowing those who control it to move instantaneously to be anywhere or nowhere. Globalization occurs in this layer, as numbers and vectors on screens control the velocity of the movements of capital, goods and information, eroding sovereignty in ways Virilio foresaw. This layer emerges from the telecommunications networks, subsea cables, landing stations, datacentres, social media platforms, 24-hour news stations, satellites, and electromagnetic waves that move between them. Instead of creating virtual worlds, we made our actual world virtual.

The stratus cloud does not float free from the earth but falls as a fog that saturates the soil, dissolving the hierarchy between virtual and actual. The virtualization layer acts on the topography it saturates, and at the same time is wholly dependent on it. It does not simply represent, manage or act upon material reality. The relation is recursive and mutually constitutive. The topography has already been formed by satellite navigation, algorithmic logistics, insurance, automated procurement, financial modelling, digital mapping and anticipatory calculation, while the virtual layer is dependent upon water, energy, minerals, cables, labor, land, climatic stability and the ability for goods to cross borders and through choke points. Neither is simply the foundation of the other. They are reciprocally interpenetrating aspects of a single dynamical system.

We are not “jacking in” to virtual worlds, like the Metaverse of Neal Stephenson’s Snow Crash or the Cyberspace of William Gibson’s Neuromancer; we are entering into Gibson’s “consensual hallucination” in this one. The tech industry has pivoted away from virtual reality devices to augmented reality glasses and other “wearables” that make the layer of virtualization permanently visible rather than accessed through ubiquitous screens that still require you to avert your vision and attention.

This symbiosis is only now being slowly understood by politicians and citizens who, having spent increasingly more time in the layer, came to see it as separate from the underlying physical reality it is situated in. In Westminster, the government fixates on the “grid,” the daily master schedule that coordinates the timing of all government announcements and media appearances in an attempt to control the news cycle and create its preferred narrative. Individuals, influencers, companies, and spy agencies compete to elevate and shape the narratives that emerge through aggregated online interactions. On the battlefield, decision-making speed and weaponry frameworks are accelerating beyond the speed of human cognition.

But unlike the pre-globalization Cold War, where competition was between two separate systems, and proxy wars could geographically fix the conflict away from the frontline of direct war, they are in competition in one global matrix.

I was taught the importance of speed through US Air Force Colonel John Boyd’s OODA Loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act). Similar to Virilio, Boyd argued that a combatant wins by operating at a faster tempo than their opponent, who is forced into a state of paralysis. When I was serving in Iraq, special forces units with dedicated helicopter assets, allowing them to move faster than their targets, looked to increase speed by exploiting intelligence found on objective to bounce on to the next target that same night. Constant efforts were made to increase the speed of human decision-making in the chain from target identification on the ground to the drone pilot in the US pulling the remote trigger. Now Western militaries believe in a future of war where algorithms fight algorithms for decision advantage at a speed humans cannot match.

The building of autonomous weapons has introduced the concept of humans being in the decision-making “loop,” “on-the-loop,” in which humans monitor and can override the autonomous system, and “off-the-loop,” in which the system makes and executes decisions autonomously without human involvement. More decision-making is being moved along the line to off-the-loop without enough consideration. As this happens, humans are being pushed out of more than just decision-making. At the Ukraine-Russia frontline, the speed of autonomous decision-making has forced soldiers from the battlefield into bunkers, as exposure results in imminent death by drone. While technological surveillance travels at the speed of light into dark corners of the globe, actual spies struggle to move as biometrics at borders restrict travel under aliases.

As we enter the Third Drone Age, characterized by full-spectrum drone warfare (FSDW), systems of autonomous air, ground and maritime machines that learn, adapt and fight as one, cutting-edge technology is increasingly being developed by off-the-loop technology. Military procurement is now as much a software problem as a hardware problem. The Ukrainian DELTA digital situational awareness ecosystem, which supports its army, was developed by the Aerorozvidka volunteer group.

The utility of commercial battlefield platforms has blurred the divide between commercial and military technology. Military–civil fusion, where commercial companies provide assets and/or services to the military and are involved on the ground floor of military technology development, has profound implications. The majority of the commercial technology militaries rely on, including civilian and military satellites and AI, are US- or Chinese-owned. Chinese companies have always operated under government sway, but now the US government is looking to take stakes in the companies driving AI innovation. They may not have full dominion over companies, but they will be able to restrict access to them.

SUGGESTED READING AI isn't a dual-use technology, it is inherently violent By Thomas Christian Bächle

These two preeminent powers are in a competition for absolute speed, manifesting in the race for AI and hypersonic ballistics. But unlike the pre-globalization Cold War, where competition was between two separate systems, and proxy wars could geographically fix the conflict away from the frontline of direct war, they are in competition in one global matrix. Every node of the matrix becomes a place of contest, every vector a way to attack. Militarily, those unable to compete are instead leveraging the asymmetry logic of the insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan. Using the speed of production, they are producing massive volumes of lower-cost commercial technologies made possible by the networks of the virtualization layer (e.g., crowd-funded drones adapted from parts ordered on Amazon based on lessons shared by social networks that stretch across borders). In Ukraine, the logic of civilian e-commerce further bleeds into the battlefield through the “Army of Drones Bonus”  program. On the Brave1 Market procurement platform, it transforms combat achievements into ePoints, virtual tokens that can be used to request and purchase custom-built drones or other military products tailored to specific tactical requirements (destroying a tank earns 20 points, a Russian soldier only 12).

They will not result in the battlefield defeat of militaries with superior technology and economic might, but it will slow them, deferring defeat, disproportionately draining their greater resources, dragging the conflict on beyond the endurance of their populations. Traditional military tactics include delaying actions, where a defending force trades space for time, slowing an advancing enemy, attriting them without becoming decisively engaged. As physical space collapses in the global matrix, adversaries are seeking to decelerate Western militaries, economies and all other societal processes, through attacking the nodes and the narratives of the layer key to advancing, in cyberspace to outer space and everywhere in between.

Unable to compete with Western military speed attacks are focussed on the critical nodes of the matrix, often where the saturation concentrates. Interconnectedness has been weaponized. Through complexity, we have built vulnerability, not resilience. In 1914, it took the Allied blockade two years before the German civilians felt the initial effects; today, algorithmic pricing instantaneously impacts consumers. Our adversaries are seeking to decelerate Western militaries, economies and all other societal processes in the layer, through attacking both the nodes and the narratives of the layer.

Iran targets data centres in the Gulf, launches cyber-attacks and blockades the straits of Hormuz spiking oil prices placing political drag on the militarily superior adversary; China restricts exports of rare earths and metals crucial for new technologies, conducts coordinated propaganda on social media and its satellites practice what the US Space Command has described as “dogfighting in space” demonstrating new capabilities to interfere with American satellites; Russia targets subsea cables, jams plane’s satellite navigation systems, and creates disinformation campaigns to propagate division; Ukraine targets oil refineries and Wildberries logistics depots inside Russia to slow its more sizeable war economy. China’s ambitions for Taiwan are of global importance not because of principles of sovereignty but due to the potential disruption of flows of chips, slowing production.

With attribution harder to determine the risk of deliberate or mistaken escalation increases.

The lines between war and peace are blurred. We are in perpetual “gray zone” conflict where sabotage, economic espionage, cyber-attacks, supply-chain infiltration, arson and assassination attack “civilian” targets, which are part of military logistics on an ever-expanding battlefield, with plausible and implausible deniability. As those who control the layer move instantaneously to be anywhere or nowhere, so can those seeking to do damage. With attribution harder to determine the risk of deliberate or mistaken escalation increases. We are simultaneously at psychic war and at peace, depending on the narrative.

Virilio warned of how new technologies change the way we see and experience the world. Technologies of speed have produced an increasingly fragmented, discontinuous, and transhistorical mode of experience that grasps instances and partial relations rather than whole fields. The virtualization layer produces a disorienting form of experience. Communication and interaction take place instantaneously in what Virilio calls “global time,” overcoming boundaries of time and space: “Here no longer exists; everything is now.” We have reached an “incessant tele-presence of events which do not really succeed each other, since the relief of instantaneity is already winning out over the depth of historical successivity.” This creates a world without reflection. Lessons of the past are wiped out as the past no longer exists. Politics is an omnishambles in an omnipresent. In war, armies no longer need to pause for rest; we have conquered sleep with autonomous systems, agentic AI and robotics.

Without referencing Boyd’s OODA Loop, Virilio argued that automated warfare completely obliterates the “Decide” phase. Real-time computerized weapon systems eliminate human reflection, turning decision-making into an instantaneous, reflex-based automation. Acceleration eliminates the mental “buffer zone” for reflection, forcing humans to act on pure reaction. Horrors like the Holocaust are marked by machine-like processes and the arbitrariness of life and death decisions. The use of landmines has resulted in conventions around their use that are not in place for other weapon systems, in part due to the absence of human decision-making at their point of use. Similar conventions are not in place for autonomous weapons. In the absence of human judgement, how can we ensure that killing is not arbitrary? When one human dehumanizes another, that person is stained in a way a machine cannot be.

This extends beyond the battlefield. Virilio claimed, “The multinational enterprise sidelines the weak at their keypads; it sidelines these new “citizens of the world” as mere consumers of a kind of parlor game in which the conditioned reflex wins out over shared reflection.” Space for democratic deliberation disappears. A form of emotivism emerges, where moral judgments are reduced to emotional attitudes of approval or disapproval, driven more by narcissism and grievance than attempts to express objective moral truths or propositions. When it is the speed with which information is transmitted and then used that is prioritized, the content becomes secondary to the medium. The disappearance of the “Decide” phase extends beyond war fighters into individual cognition of civilians, many of whom have also handed over the “Observe” and “Orient” phases to algorithms.

States and non-state groups are taking advantage of the disorienting effects of technology and magnifying them. Emotions are manipulated through disinformation and misinformation at a speed that does not allow reflection. Stuck in an ahistorical “global time,” the speed of our politics is bringing our ability to govern for the future to a standstill. China’s ability to plan on a timeline far beyond American election cycles gives it a consequential advantage. Insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan refused to fight in global time, pulling the coalition into their local time, using ancient concepts which have fallen out of our lexicon like honor, God and sacred land, providing their people deeper historical narratives to steel them for a fight on a grand timescale Western civilian populations can no longer understand.

However, much of the disorientation we experience is self-inflicted. Technology is accelerating existing recursive bureaucratic, logistic and economic systems that increasingly feel outside the influence of human agency. As we see an exponential automatization of these recursive systems, our idea of ourselves is being modified (the brain as a computer; the human as a technology-enabled economic agent) and our intentionality reduced.

While Virilio focuses on speed, writer Will Self builds on his ideas to focus on the autonomous, recursive loop represented by the drone, where surveillance, action, and media broadcast happen simultaneously in real time. In his forthcoming book The Gulf War Did Take Place... The Gulf War is Taking Place... The Gulf War Will Always be Taking Place... (SITREP: The Always-already Era of Dromodronology), Self coins the term “dromodronology,” claiming that what looks like sovereign intention is increasingly a distributed pseudo-intentionality arising across institutions, machines, markets, protocols, and human beings that causes an erasure of agency. Humans are removed or bypassed, becoming components or consumers in a closed loop of disaggregated innumerable nodes.

Self told me that the experience of Afghanistan described in my 2006 book Land of the Blind already contains dromodronological ideas: “The base exists to support the troops, while the troops exist to defend the base; intelligence requested for an operational purpose is supplied by a compromised source, recirculated through another agency, and returned as independent corroboration; development money indirectly sustains those attacking the development mission…. The mission has ceased to determine the system’s operation, while the system’s continued operation retrospectively supplies the mission.”

Reality abounds with stochastic processes. There are still nodes of the power.

Some of Keir Starmer’s unpopularity was due to the backlash against the technocratic class he represented, but the anger toward him, the “empty suit,” was likely due to a subconscious recognition of our own lack of agency in a declining, hollowed out, state. UK politicians are helpless to influence a macro-environment that restricts their ability to set national policies. Executive authorities attempting to float free from lived social embeddedness while still attempting to simulate it theatrically in a virtualization layer they conceive as separate from the material world are finding there is a limit to how much you can convince people to ignore the physical reality they are experiencing. As the cost of living increases and opportunities for the many decrease in the shadow of the few’s accumulating wealth, and governments fail in their responsibility to provide security for their citizens, we are pushing up against that limit.

Self does not argue that there is no agency. There are always accidental factors. Reality abounds with stochastic processes. There are still nodes of the power. Despite America’s waning hegemony, President Trump has agency to set events in motion, if not decisively determine them, generating unintended consequences. Trump is drawn to autocrats due to their egoism, but also their greater agency (he is part of a system that limits political power despite democratic erosion). The decisions of despots, their ability to manipulate Trump, and Trump’s own emotive reactions all do change the course of events. What Self claims is that what appears retrospectively as a decision by a sovereign actor is frequently the emergent result of a system no one component comprehends or commands. As Self tells me, increasingly individuals are “capable of amplifying, damping or redirecting currents, sometimes with catastrophic consequences, but unable to comprehend or command the system as a whole.” Historically, conflicts are avoided by balances of power; if there is no real agency to balance such distributed power, the risk of spiralling conflict increases.

Ultimately, what may alter our course more is Virilio’s “accident to end all accidents.” For Virilio, every technology involves its accompanying accident: with the invention of the ship, you get the shipwreck; the plane brings on plane crashes; instant algorithmic trading brings a new type of financial crash. He draws an analogy between the nuclear bomb, which uses radioactive energy to destroy matter, and the “information bomb,” which uses the interactivity of information to cause chaos. Such an accident could be the ultimate deliberately instigated deceleration. It’s mistaken attribution an accelerator for wider conflict. Alternatively, it may be just the slow self-inflicted accumulation of slop and disorientation that slows us down. Every abundance creates its opposite. Scientist David C. Krakauer argues that stupidity is not the absence of intelligence, but its “evil twin.” You need high intelligence to produce true, consequential stupidity. Super intelligence can lead to super stupidity.

Aspects of Virilio’s dystopian vision have come to pass. However, the space and time saturated by the virtualization layer remains far from obsolete. As the Allied bombing of the factories of the Ruhr Valley attacked Germany’s logistical nodes and the 9/11 attacks targeted a key financial node of the global economy, new physical nodes of the hyperconnected, high-velocity, multimatrixed world are being attacked in attempts to decelerate those travelling at the greatest velocity.

Virilio advocated for a societal voluntary technological regression. As geopolitical competition intensifies, it’s unlikely governments will voluntarily hit the brakes on technological development (commercial ownership of such technology will also complicate any attempts). So, while governments grapple with new challenges of national resiliency, ensuring external forces do not decelerate relied-upon technology, we need to reclaim what agency we can.

We should begin by recognizing that technology should not replace thought. Doing things at greater speed does not help us resolve the diverging ideals and norms within and between societies. Neither technocratic government that assumes a consensus on values that does not exist, nor technological logistic systems can do this. Neither relieve us of accountability or our civic duty to insist our governments use what remains of their diminishing sovereignty agency.

As individuals, we must create space for personal and democratic reflection and discretion. We must take responsibility for thinking deeply about how we mediate the conflicts of interests and values, and how we solve global problems that the logistical systems we have created have no short-term incentive to solve, such as the climate emergency. Self urges us to consider the existential consequences of not conducting selective technological decomplexification. If we don’t, either deliberate attack, accident, or the pushing against ecological limits will force a deceleration outside of our control. Deceleration is more hazardous than acceleration. After all, it is not the fall that kills you—it’s hitting the ground.

Will Self’s The Gulf War Did Take Place... The Gulf War is Taking Place... The Gulf War Will Always be Taking Place... (SITREP: The Always-already Era of Dromodronology) will be out in September.
